# Introduction

## Background: Cardiomyopathy

Cardiomyopathy is a group of diseases that affect the heart muscle, leading to structural and functional abnormalities that impair the heart’s ability to pump blood efficiently. These conditions can result in serious clinical outcomes, including heart failure, arrhythmias, and sudden cardiac death.

Many forms of cardiomyopathy have a genetic basis. Inherited mutations have been associated with several types of the disease, such as hypertrophic, dilated, restrictive, and arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy, as well as left ventricular non-compaction and ion channelopathies. These mutations often affect genes involved in heart muscle structure and function, including those related to the sarcomere, cytoskeleton, and ion channels.

## Aim and Research Questions

The aim of this project is to identify and evaluate genetic variants associated with cardiomyopathy using DNA sequencing data. By comparing the patient’s DNA sequence to established cardiomyopathy-associated gene panels, potentially pathogenic variants can be detected and assessed. Using next-generation sequencing (NGS) technologies, this project seeks to identify genetic variants that may contribute to the development and progression of cardiomyopathy and to evaluate their relevance in a diagnostic context.

# Materials and Methods

## Dataset Description

### Data Source

The dataset used in this project consists of DNA sequencing data obtained from patients diagnosed with cardiomyopathy. The data were provided as part of a master-level genomics course and were used for educational and research purposes.

### Number of Samples

> The dataset consists of multiple patient samples derived from cardiomyopathy cases. In this project, the analysis focuses on **Sample 1**, which is provided as paired-end sequencing data consisting of two read files (forward and reverse reads).

Version control and collaboration were managed using **GitHub**, allowing transparent tracking of changes and shared development of the analysis. **Microsoft Teams** was used as the primary communication platform to coordinate the workflow, discuss results, and share progress with each other and with the course instructor.

# Analysis Workflow

The overall analysis workflow is designed to identify and characterize genetic variants from DNA sequencing data in a systematic and reproducible manner. The workflow includes quality control of raw reads, read preprocessing, alignment to a reference genome, variant calling, and variant filtering and annotation. Each step of the analysis is briefly introduced here and discussed in detail in the following subsections.

## Quality Control of Raw Reads

Quality control of raw sequencing reads was performed to evaluate data quality before downstream analysis. For this purpose, the tool **Falco** was used. A `.fastQ.gz` file was provided as input, and Falco generates several plots as output. Each plot highlights a specific aspect of the sequencing data, such as base quality scores, GC content, sequence length distribution, and the presence of adapter contamination, and provides a quality assessment in the form of **pass, warn, or fail**.

### Quality Control Results \*\* Here will add the results for r1 also! \*\*

The quality control results were examined to determine whether read trimming or filtering was required before alignment. Key observations from the quality reports are summarized and interpreted in this section.

### Basic Statistics

| Measure                           | Value                                |
|-----------------------------------|--------------------------------------|
| Filename                          | Sample1_0394321_L001_R1_001_fastq_gz |
| File type                         | Conventional base calls              |
| Encoding                          | Sanger / Illumina 1.9                |
| Total Sequences                   | 1424257                              |
| Sequences Flagged As Poor Quality | 0                                    |
| Sequence length                   | 32 - 151                             |
| %GC:                              | 43                                   |

## **Per base sequence quality: pass**

Per-base sequence quality refers to the assessment of quality scores for each nucleotide position in sequencing reads. This was evaluated using Falco, which generates a box-and-whisker plot showing Phred scores across all read positions. According to FastQC standards, a warning is issued if the lower quartile falls below 10 or the median falls below 25, whereas a failure is reported if the lower quartile falls below 5 or the median falls below **20**. The results show that all base positions in our data have quality scores ranging from **33.0 to 44.0**, which is well above both warning and failure thresholds. This indicates that our sequencing data pass the quality control check with high confidence in base-calling accuracy across all positions.

![](./assets/quality_res_byROA/Per%20base%20sequence%20quality1.png)

## **Per tile sequence quality : pass**

Per tile sequence quality examines quality variation between different tiles on the flow cell using a color scale where blue indicates average or above-average quality and red indicates lower quality. A warning is issued if any tile falls more than **2** Phred scores below the mean, and failure if more than **5** below. Our results show consistent blue coloration across all tiles with no significant deviations, confirming that the data **passes** this quality control check.

![](./assets/quality_res_byROA/Per%20tile%20sequence%20quality1.png)

## **Per sequence quality scores : pass**

Per sequence quality scores examine whether subsets of sequences have universally low quality values, which may indicate systematic issues like poor imaging at flow cell edges. A warning is issued if the most frequently observed mean quality falls below **27 (0.2% error rate)**, and failure occurs below **20 (1% error rate)**. In our results, the majority of sequences have mean quality scores above 30, well above both thresholds, confirming that the data passes this quality check.

![](./assets/quality_res_byROA/Per%20sequence%20quality%20scores1.png)

## **Per base sequence content : fail**

Per base sequence content analyzes the proportion of each nucleotide (A, T, C, G) at every position across all reads. In a properly balanced library, the lines for each base should run parallel with only small differences between A and T or G and C. A warning is issued if the difference between A and T or G and C exceeds **10%** at any position, and failure occurs if the difference exceeds **20%**.

![](./assets/quality_res_byROA/Per%20base%20sequence%20content1.png)

In our results, the data failed this module. As shown, there is a consistent imbalance between A and T across most positions, with A averaging around **29%** while T averages only **21%**, creating a difference of approximately **8%**. While this difference is below the failure threshold, it still exceeds the warning threshold, indicating a systematic bias in nucleotide distribution that may need to be addressed before further analysis.

## **Per sequence GC content: pass**

Per sequence GC content measures the distribution of G and C bases across all reads, plotted as the number of reads versus GC percentage. A normal distribution is expected for high-quality data, with the peak matching the genome's overall GC content.

![](./assets/quality_res_byROA/Per%20sequence%20GC%20content1.png)

Our results passed this module, showing a GC distribution that closely follows the theoretical distribution. As shown, the highest density of reads occurs at **50-60%** GC, which aligns well with the expected pattern for this dataset. This indicates no significant GC bias in the sequencing data.

## **Per base N content : pass**

Per base N content measures the proportion of ambiguous base calls (N) at each position across all reads. Low N content, especially near read ends, is normal and expected. A warning is issued if any position exceeds **5%** N content, and failure occurs if above **20%**. Our results passed this module, with N content remaining consistently low **(below 0.04%)** across all positions. This indicates high-quality base calling with minimal ambiguity throughout the sequencing run.

![](./assets/quality_res_byROA/Per%20base%20N%20content1.png)

## **Sequence Length Distribution : warn**

Sequence length distribution analyzes the range of fragment sizes in the raw sequencing data. A warning is issued if all sequences are not the same length, while failure occurs if any sequence has zero length. Our results show a warning in this module, indicating that the reads in our raw dataset are not all identical in length.

![](./assets/quality_res_byROA/Sequence%20Length%20Distribution1.png)

## **Sequence Duplication Levels : warn**

Sequence duplication levels measure the proportion of duplicate reads in the sequencing data. This module identifies reads that appear more than once, which can indicate over-amplification during library preparation. A warning is issued when non-unique reads make up more than **20%** of the total sequences. Our results show a warning in this module, indicating a moderate level of duplication in the dataset.

![](./assets/quality_res_byROA/Sequence%20Duplication%20Levels1.png)

## **Overrepresented sequences : pass**

Overrepresented sequences are those that appear more frequently than expected in the dataset. Our results passed this module as no overrepresented sequences were found.

## **Adapter Content : pass**

Adapter content assesses the presence of adapter sequences in the reads, which can occur when fragments are shorter than the read length. A warning is issued if any adapter is present in more than **5%** of reads, and failure occurs if above **10%**. Our results passed this module with very low adapter content **(below 0.8%)** across all positions, indicating minimal adapter contamination.

![](./assets/quality_res_byROA/Adapter%20Content1.png)

## Read Trimming and Filtering (**we can use the jero table)**

Based on the initial quality assessment, reads were trimmed to remove low-quality bases and sequencing adapters, ensuring that only high-quality sequences were retained for downstream analysis.

**Tool used:** (`Trimmomatic`)

### Trimming Parameters

Based on our quality control results, we selected specific parameters for trimming with Trimmomatic. We kept the default values for the adapter clipping settings, and added several parameters to address issues identified in the quality report: we applied CROP to 145 bases to remove positions beyond 145 that showed noise in the per base sequence content, used HEADCROP of 7 bases to eliminate low-quality bases from the read starts, and set MINLEN to 50 to discard short reads after trimming, ensuring high-quality data for subsequent analysis.

**Tool Parameters**

| Input Parameter | Value |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| Single-end or paired-end reads? | pair_of_files |
| Input FASTQ file (R1/first of pair) |  |
| Input FASTQ file (R2/second of pair) |  |
| Perform initial ILLUMINACLIP step? | true |
| Select standard adapter sequences or provide custom? | standard |
| Adapter sequences to use | TruSeq3 (paired-ended, for MiSeq and HiSeq) |
| Maximum mismatch count which will still allow a full match to be performed | 2 |
| How accurate the match between the two 'adapter ligated' reads must be for PE palindrome read alignment | 30 |
| How accurate the match between any adapter etc. sequence must be against a read | 10 |
| Minimum length of adapter that needs to be detected (PE specific/palindrome mode) | 8 |
| Always keep both reads (PE specific/palindrome mode)? | true |
| Select Trimmomatic operation to perform | SLIDINGWINDOW |

## Read Alignment (mapping with jero)

Filtered reads were aligned to the appropriate human reference genome using a short-read aligner.

**Reference genome:**

**Alignment tool: BWA**

### Alignment Statistics

Key alignment metrics such as mapping rate and coverage were evaluated.

coverage with jero !

### Marking Duplicate Mapped Reads

Before analyzing differences between the reference genome and our patient sample, duplicate mapped reads must be identified. Duplicates arise from PCR amplification bias (multiple copies of the same fragment) or optical artifacts during sequencing, and if unaddressed, can lead to false positive variant calls and inaccurate coverage estimates.

We used `MarkDuplicates` tool on the coordinate-sorted BAM files from the previous mapping step. The algorithm identifies duplicate pairs by comparing read coordinates, orientations, and insert sizes, then adds a duplicate flag to each identified duplicate read. Importantly, reads are flagged but not removed, preserving data integrity while allowing downstream tools to ignore these flagged reads during analysis.

**The output includes:**

A marked BAM file `.marked.bam`: alignment data with duplicate flags

A BAM index file `.bai`: enables rapid random access for visualization

These files serve as input for the next step: visualizing the mapping data without the confounding effects of duplicates.

### Visualizing the Mapping Data

#### Integrative Genomics Viewer (IGV)

To visually inspect the mapped reads and identify potential variants, we used the **Integrative Genomics Viewer (IGV)**. This tool enabled visualization of read alignment, coverage depth, and nucleotide changes across target regions, using the BED file to navigate directly to genes of interest.

#### Reference Genome and Data Files

The reference genome used for visualization was **GRCh38/hg38** (Genome Reference Consortium Human Build 38), which provides a high-quality assembly of the human genome. 

For this visualization step, we used two primary input files:

1.  **Marked BAM file** (`dataset.bam`): Contains the aligned reads with duplicate flags, enabling accurate visualization without PCR bias.

2.  **Target BED file** (`CAR_0394321_en-20_target_v2_8.bed`): A interval file specifying all captured regions in the gene panel.

The BED file contains four columns specifying the chromosome, exon start and end positions, and gene name (e.g., PSEN2, LMNA), allowing us to navigate directly to regions of interest. This BED file served as a navigation guide, allowing us to rapidly zoom into specific genes of interest and examine their coverage and potential variants.

#### Variant Identification

Using the BED file to navigate, we examined two different genes of interest. Below are representative examples of variants identified in this analysis:

**Figure 1: PSEN2 Gene Region**

![](./assets/quality_res_byROA/mapping/varient%20on%20stop%20codon.jpeg)

A variant was identified in the PSEN2 gene at the stop codon position. The reference sequence shows a stop codon (TGA), while the patient sample displays a T nucleotide (red) at this position, changing the codon to CGA, which encodes Arginine (ARG). This stop-loss variant would result in an extended protein product, potentially altering its normal function.

**Figure 2: LMNA Gene Region**

![](./assets/quality_res_byROA/mapping/3.jpeg)

Visualization of the LMNA gene showing a heterozygous variant. The aligned reads display both reference and alternative alleles (mixed colors at the variant position), with approximately equal representation. Heterozygous variants in LMNA are known to be associated with dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM).

## Mapping Quality Control

In this section, we assessed the mapping coverage for all panel genes to evaluate mapping performance. As observed in IGV, coverage levels varied significantly across regions, ranging from very high (300+) to areas with only a few reads present, which can impact variant detection reliability. Using **R** with libraries commonly used in genetic research, we calculated and reported coverage statistics for all panel genes to quantitatively assess these variations and identify undercovered regions.

### Loading the BED-data

The first step is to load the BED file containing the exon coordinates of our panel genes. The file is tab-separated and has four columns: chromosome, start, end, and gene name. We will read it into R, assign proper column names, and then examine the distribution of exons across chromosomes.

```{r}

bed_file <- "./BedFile.bed"

exons <- read.table(bed_file, header = FALSE, sep = "\t", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

colnames(exons) <- c("chromosome", "start", "end", "gene")

head(exons)
#View(exons)

# Count exons per chromosome
exon_counts <- table(exons$chromosome)
print(exon_counts)

# Plot the number of exons per chromosome
barplot(exon_counts, 
        main = "Number of exons per chromosome",
        ylab = "Exon count",
        xlab = "Chromosome",
        las = 2,
)       

```

This barplot shows the number of exons located on each chromosome in our dataset. Chromosomes with higher exon counts typically contain more genes or longer genes with multiple exons. For example, chromosome 2 has the highest exon count (around 250-300). In contrast, chromosomes like chr18, chr20, and chrX have fewer exons, indicating they may contain fewer genes or genes with simpler structures.


### BED-visualization

In this section, we visualized the distribution of genes across different chromosomes using the BED data. First, we reduced the data to unique chromosome-gene combinations, then counted the number of genes per chromosome and presented the results in a bar plot. This visualization provides a clear overview of how genes are distributed across chromosomes, helping to identify which chromosomes carry the most genes in our panel.

```{r}
chromosome_gene <- subset(exons, select = c(chromosome, gene))
head(chromosome_gene)

uni_gene <- unique(chromosome_gene)

head(uni_gene)
#View(uni_gene)

gene_counts <- table(uni_gene$chromosome)

barplot(gene_counts, 
        main = "Number of gene per chromosome",
        ylab = "Number of genes",
        xlab = "Chromosome",
        las = 2,
    )
```

This plot shows the number of genes per chromosome, and it directly explains the previous exon distribution. Chromosome 2 has the highest gene count (7 genes), which is why it also had the highest exon count (250-300). Chromosomes with fewer genes consistently showed fewer exons, confirming that exon numbers reflect gene density across chromosomes.

### Bioconductor

Bioconductor is a repository containing over 1800 R packages specifically designed for analyzing high-throughput biological data, which we used throughout this assignment.

**Why Convert IRanges to GRanges?**

The IRanges object contains exon positions and lengths but lacks chromosome information, making it incomplete for genomic analysis. Converting to a GRanges object adds the chromosome context, creating a complete genomic coordinate system that properly locates each exon in the genome.

### GenomicRanges objects

The BED file was first represented as an IRanges object since it contains simple positional data such as chromosome names and start/stop positions. These IRanges objects were then converted to GenomicRanges objects, which store genomic features (like exons) along with their chromosome coordinates and strand information.

```{r}
# Split the data by gene, resulting in a list with named elements
library(IRanges)
library(GenomicRanges)

bed_splitted <- split(exons, exons$gene)
#View(bed_splitted)
my_list <- list()

for (gene in names(bed_splitted)[1:55]) {
  
  data <- bed_splitted[[gene]]

  ranges <- IRanges(start = data$start,
                  end = data$end, names = data$gene)
  #print(ranges)
 granges <- GRanges(seqnames = data$chromosome,
                   ranges = ranges) 
 
 my_list[[gene]] <- granges

}

final_GRange_list <- GRangesList(my_list) 

#class(final_GRange_list)
#elementType(final_GRange_list)

head(final_GRange_list)

```

### Gene Lengths Visualization

After creating the GRanges objects, we calculated the length of each gene using the width and sum functions on the GRangesList. Since some genes are much longer than others, a standard barplot would be difficult to read. We used the `gap.barplot` function from the plotrix library, which allows us to create a barplot with a gap in the y-axis to accommodate extremely long genes while still showing variation among shorter genes.

```{r}
library(plotrix)

# sapply applies the function to each element and returns a vector
gene_lengths <- sapply(names(final_GRange_list), function(gene) {
  gene_ranges <- ranges(final_GRange_list[[gene]])
  sum(width(gene_ranges))
})


gene_lengths <- sort(gene_lengths, decreasing = TRUE)

# Create barplot
gap.barplot(gene_lengths,
            gap = c(5000, 80000),
            xlab = "Genes",
            ylab = "Gene Length (bp)",
            main = "Gene Lengths Distribution",
            las = 2, 
            ytics = seq(0, 100000, by = 5000))

```

```{r}
# Simple barplot with more tick marks
barplot(gene_lengths,
        xlab = "Genes",
        ylab = "Gene Length (bp)",
        main = "Gene Lengths Distribution",
        las = 2,
        ylim = c(0, 100000),
        yaxt = "n")  # Remove default y-axis

# Add custom y-axis
axis(2, at = seq(0, 100000, by = 5000), las = 2)
```

### Loading the Mapped Reads

We used the output from the mapping step (the BAM file) to inspect the coverage of all mapped positions across our panel genes. The Rsamtools library provides the necessary functions to read and process this alignment data into GRanges objects for further analysis.

First, we used the *BamFile* function to create a reference to our BAM file and its index, which allowed us to access the alignment data efficiently without loading the entire file into memory. Then, to extract only our specific gene regions from the BED-data, we used the *ScanBamParam* function with GRanges objects to set the parameters for selection. Finally, we applied the *pileup* function to retrieve the coverage information for these regions, which returned the actual read counts at each position within our genes for downstream analysis. Here the pileup data for **TTN** gene.

```{r}
# Loading the RSamtools library
library(Rsamtools)

bam_file <- BamFile(file="./mapping.bam", index = "./mapping.bam.bai")

TTN_gene <- final_GRange_list[["TTN"]]

ScanParam_gene <-ScanBamParam(which = TTN_gene)

pileup_data <- pileup(file = bam_file, scanBamParam = ScanParam_gene)

head(pileup_data)


```

### Pileup Processing

Here, we will obtain the pileup data for all our genes and store it in a single object `pileup_list`. This will allow us to calculate the average coverage for each gene and identify positions with low coverage that may require further inspection.

```{r}
pileup_list <- list()

for (gene in names(final_GRange_list)) {
  
  data <- final_GRange_list[[gene]]

 ScanParam_gene <-ScanBamParam(which = data)

pileup_data <- pileup(file = bam_file, scanBamParam = ScanParam_gene)
 
 pileup_list[[gene]] <- pileup_data

}
head(pileup_list[["TTN"]])
```

This table shows the raw sequencing data for every position in our genes. Each row represents one nucleotide position, telling us which chromosome it's on, the exact location, which DNA strand the read came from, what base (A, T, G, or C) was detected, and how many times that base was seen. The last column just labels which gene the position belongs to. This data helps us see how well each region was covered during sequencing and spot any positions that might need a closer look.

### Coverage calculation and reporting

In this assignment, we calculated the per-position coverage for each gene using the *aggregate* function, which sums the count values for each unique position across all reads. For every gene, we then determined: the number of bases sequenced, the average coverage, the number of low-coverage positions (below 30), and the percentage of low-coverage positions. These four values were stored in a new data frame along with the gene name, and the final results were ordered by the percentage of low-coverage positions in descending order for easy interpretation.

```{r}
options(stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

per_position_coverage <- data.frame(Gene = character(),
                           NumBases = integer(),
                           AvgCoverage = numeric(),
                           LowCovPos = integer(),
                           LowCovPerc = numeric())

for (gene_name in names(pileup_list)) {
  
  gene_data <- pileup_list[[gene_name]]
  
  coverage <- aggregate(x = list(count = gene_data$count),
                       by = list(pos = gene_data$pos),
                       FUN = sum)
  
  num_bases <- nrow(coverage)
  avg_cov <- mean(coverage$count)
  low_cov_num <- sum(coverage$count < 30)
  low_cov_perc <- (low_cov_num / num_bases) * 100
  
  new_row <- list(Gene = gene_name,
                  NumBases = num_bases,
                  AvgCoverage = avg_cov,
                  LowCovPos = low_cov_num,
                  LowCovPerc = low_cov_perc)
  
  per_position_coverage <- rbind(per_position_coverage, new_row)
  
}

print("All genes processed:")
print(per_position_coverage)

```

Coverage analysis across the 55 cardiomyopathy genes shows that the majority **(40 genes)** have excellent sequencing coverage with **0%** low coverage positions. However, several genes show concerning coverage gaps. JPH2 has the poorest coverage with **(30.7%)** of the gene falling below acceptable thresholds, followed by GATAD1 **(21.3%)**, TPM1 **(16.8%)**, and PRKAG2 **(16.3%)**. Other genes with significant coverage issues include DES **(14.7%)**, JUP **(11.2%)**, and MYBPC3 **(10.5%)**. These genes with \>10% low coverage warrant careful interpretation as potential variants in these poorly covered regions may be missed. In contrast, important large genes like TTN maintained excellent coverage throughout, increasing confidence in variant detection.

## Variant Calling

Variant calling was performed to identify single nucleotide variants (SNVs) and small insertions/deletions (indels) from the aligned reads. We interest in a SNVs variants only, and using the default sittings in the tool.

**Variant caller used: `Call variants with LoFreq`**

### Raw Variant Output (VCF File)

The result of the `LoFreq` tool is a single new file in your history in the vcf file format where each line describes a single variant. We have **1005** different variants.

```{r}
library(readr)
VCF_FILE <- read.delim("Call_variants.vcf", stringsAsFactors = FALSE , comment = "#")

head(VCF_FILE)
```

## Variant Filtering (VCF File Processing)

To minimize false positive calls, variants were filtered using established quality metrics, including read depth, variant quality score, and allele frequency. The filtering workflow began by extracting allele frequency (AF) information from the VCF file. This AF data was subsequently incorporated as an additional column following the creation of GRanges objects.

```{r}

vcfInfo <- do.call(rbind,
  strsplit(VCF_FILE$INFO, ";"))

vcfInfo <- data.frame(vcfInfo)
names(vcfInfo) <- c("DP", "AF", "SB", "DP4")

alleleFreq <- as.numeric(gsub("AF=", x = vcfInfo$AF, ""))


```

Variants were subsequently filtered to retain only those with an allele frequency of ≥30%.

```{r}
#VCF_FILE

vcfIRanges <- IRanges(start = VCF_FILE$POS, end = VCF_FILE$POS)

vcfGRanges <- GRanges(seqnames = VCF_FILE$CHROM, ranges = vcfIRanges )

mcols(vcfGRanges) <- DataFrame(AF = alleleFreq)


vcfGRanges <- vcfGRanges[vcfGRanges$AF >= 0.3]

vcfGRanges
```

To identify all variants falling within exonic regions, an overlap analysis was performed using the `findOverlaps` function. The resulting output contains two columns: `queryHits` and `subjectHits.` The `queryHits` column indicates the rows from the VCF data that lie within an exon, representing the variants of interest. The `subjectHits` column corresponds not to individual exons but to genes, meaning a `subjectHits` value of 1 refers to a hit within any exon of the first gene.

From the results, gene number 25 was observed to have 21 hits within its exonic regions.

```{r}
overlaps <- findOverlaps(vcfGRanges, final_GRange_list)
overlaps <- DataFrame(overlaps)
(overlaps)


```

After obtaining the row numbers of variants to retain, the filtered VCF file was reconstructed. This was achieved by reading the original VCF file with the readLines function. The header lines and variant rows were extracted separately, then recombined to generate the final filtered VCF file.

```{r}
vcfLines <- readLines(con = file("./Call_variants.vcf"))

header_lines <- vcfLines[1:146]

variant_lines <- vcfLines[147:length(vcfLines)]

final_vcf <- c(header_lines, variant_lines)

writeLines(final_vcf, "filtered_variants.vcf")


#cat("Original total lines:", length(vcfLines), "\n")
#cat("Header lines:", length(header_lines), "\n")
#cat("Original variants:", length(variant_lines), "\n")
#cat("New file total lines:", length(final_vcf), "\n")

```

## Variant Visualization

Two simple visualizations were created to explore the filtered variant dataset.

### Allele frequency distribution

```{r}
hist(alleleFreq, breaks = 20, main = "Distribution of Allele Frequencies",
     xlab = "Allele Frequency",
     ylab = "Number of Variants",
     col = "steelblue")
```

The two peaks in the allele frequency histogram correspond to the two possible zygosity states in a diploid genome:

-   **50%**: Heterozygous variants, where one copy carries the alternative allele and the other carries the reference allele

-   **100%**: Homozygous variants, where both copies carry the alternative allele

### Variants per gene

```{r}

variantFreq <- table(overlaps$subjectHits)

names(variantFreq) <- names(final_GRange_list)[as.integer(names(variantFreq))]

variantFreq <- data.frame(variantFreq)

names(variantFreq) <- c("gene_name", "variant_count")

#variantFreq
#barplot(table(overlaps$subjectHits))

ggplot(variantFreq, aes(x = gene_name, y = variant_count, fill = gene_name)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Number of Variants per Gene", x = "Genes", y = "Number of Variants") +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 20, by = 2)) +   # finer y‑axis breaks
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 20)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1, vjust = 0.5))  # vertical labels


```

Looking at the distribution of variants across genes, **TTN** had the highest number with 19 variants, followed by **RYR2** with 11. **MYPN** and **DMD** each had 10 variants, while **MYH6** had 8. A few other genes like **DSP** (6) and **DES** (5) also showed moderate variant counts. The rest of the genes had smaller numbers, mostly between 1 and 3 variants.

What's interesting is that most of the genes with the highest variant counts are actually known to be involved in heart disease. So even though the variants are spread across many genes, the ones with the most hits tend to be those with known roles in cardiac function. This is not surprising, as our samples were obtained from patients with cardiomyopathy, so finding more variants in heart-disease-associated genes is expected.

## Variant Annotation

The filtered VCF file was uploaded to Galaxy for the subsequent annotation step to identify and characterize the genetic differences.

### SnpEff and SnpSift

Following variant calling with `LoFreq`, we performed three sequential annotation steps to add functional, clinical, and population-level information to our filtered VCF file.

**SnpEff – Functional Annotation**

We used `SnpEff` with the GRCh38.p14 genome reference to annotate our filtered VCF file. This tool adds functional predictions for each variant, including impact severity (HIGH, MODERATE, LOW, MODIFIER), gene names, transcript biotypes, and HGVS nomenclature. All annotation details are stored in the `ANN` field. The output consists of an annotated VCF file and a web-based summary report.

**SnpSift – dbSNP and ClinVar Annotation**

We ran `SnpSift` to add known variant identifiers and clinical significance data using the `dbSNP` database that includes `ClinVar` information. The `ID` column was populated with ClinVar identifiers, and the `INFO` field was expanded with clinical significance (CLNSIG), disease names (CLNDN), and review status (CLNREVSTAT) for known variants.

**SnpSift – dbNSFP Annotation**

We used `SnpSift` to annotate our VCF with the `dbNSFP` database, a comprehensive collection of over 300GB of integrated annotation sources. This step added population allele frequencies from gnomAD and ExAC, multiple in-silico prediction scores (including SIFT, PolyPhen, REVEL, CADD, and AlphaMissense), conservation metrics, and gene constraint information. The resulting file, `SnpVariants_Step3.vcf`, was used for subsequent filtering and analysis in Galaxy.

**Annotation Summary**

After completing the annotation workflow in Galaxy, we performed additional processing in R to extract and summarize the metadata from our annotated VCF file. The final output consolidates the key annotation data added during each step of the workflow. A brief summary of the added annotation sources and the types of values they provide is presented in the table below.


### Analyzing Variant Annotation

After annotating our VCF file with functional, clinical, and population-level data, we performed additional data preparation steps to convert the complex annotation fields into a workable format suitable for filtering and ranking in R.

**Data Preparation**

-   Step #1 & #2; SnpEff ANN data and SnpSift ClinVar data

We used the `SnpSift` Extract Fields tool in Galaxy to extract specific annotation fields from the annotated VCF file into a tabular format. This tool allows us to parse the complex `ANN` field—which contains multiple sub-fields separated by pipes (\|)—and convert them into individual columns. We enabled the "One effect per line" option, which creates a separate row for each transcript effect reported by `SnpEff`, ensuring that no annotation data is lost. The selected fields included basic variant information (CHROM, POS, ID, REF, ALT, FILTER) along with key SnpEff annotations such as effect type, impact severity, gene name, feature type, feature ID, and biotype, as well as ClinVar fields (CLNDN, CLNSIG, CLNVC). This produced our first tabular file containing functional and clinical annotations.

-   Step #3; SnpSift dbNSFP

Similarly, we used the `SnpSift` Extract Fields tool to extract `dbNSFP` annotations from the VCF file. All `dbNSFP` fields are prefixed with `dbNSFP_`, allowing us to selectively extract population frequencies, prediction scores, and conservation metrics. We extracted fields including population allele frequency (ExAC_Adj_AF), ensemble predictions (MetaSVM_pred), protein domain information (Interpro_domain), evolutionary predictions (LRT_pred), conservation scores (phastCons100way_vertebrate), and multiple in-silico predictors (MutationTaster_pred, MutationAssessor_pred, SIFT_pred). This produced a second tabular file containing comprehensive population and deleteriousness annotations.

-   Merging and Column Selection

After generating two separate tabular files—one containing SnpEff and ClinVar data, and another containing dbNSFP data—we merged them into a single consolidated file for analysis in R. The final merged file includes the following selected columns:

| Column | Reason for Inclusion |
|---------------------|---------------------------------------------------|
| CHROM, POS, ID, REF, ALT, FILTER | Core variant identification and quality control |
| ANN[\*].EFFECT | Specific molecular consequence (e.g., missense, stop_gained) |
| ANN[\*].IMPACT | Severity ranking (HIGH, MODERATE, LOW, MODIFIER) |
| ANN[\*].GENE | Gene symbol for biological context |
| ANN[\*].FEATURE | Feature type (transcript, regulatory region) |
| ANN[\*].FEATUREID | Unique transcript identifier for cross-referencing |
| ANN[\*].BIOTYPE | Transcript classification (protein_coding, pseudogene) |
| CLNDN, CLNSIG, CLNVC | Clinical significance and disease associations from ClinVar |
| dbNSFP_REVEL_score | Ensemble meta-predictor for missense pathogenicity |
| dbNSFP_SIFT_pred, dbNSFP_SIFT_score | SIFT prediction and score for missense deleteriousness |
| dbNSFP_Polyphen2_HDIV_pred, dbNSFP_Polyphen2_HVAR_pred | Polyphen2 predictions (human diversity and human variation modes) |
| dbNSFP_MutationTaster_pred | Comprehensive disease-causing prediction |
| dbNSFP_CADD_phred | Combined Annotation Dependent Depletion (CADD) phred score for variant deleteriousness |
| dbNSFP_VEST4_score | Variant Effect Scoring Tool (VEST4) for missense pathogenicity |
| dbNSFP_ESM1b_pred | Evolutionary Scale Modeling (ESM1b) prediction for protein variant effects |
| dbNSFP_phyloP100way_vertebrate | Phylogenetic conservation score across 100 vertebrates |
| dbNSFP_GERP___NR, dbNSFP_GERP___RS | Genomic Evolutionary Rate Profiling (GERP) rejected substitutions and neutral rate scores |
| dbNSFP_fathmm_XF_coding_pred | Functional Analysis Through Hidden Markov Models (fathmm) coding variant prediction |
| dbNSFP_BayesDel_addAF_pred | Bayesian deleteriousness prediction incorporating allele frequency |
| dbNSFP_MetaSVM_pred, dbNSFP_MetaLR_pred | Ensemble SVM and logistic regression meta-predictors for missense impact |

```{r}

snpFilteredVariants_1 <- read.table("./FilteredTEST.tabular", sep = "", quote = "", fill = T, header = T)
#View(snpFilteredVariants_1)

```

**Finding Variants of Interest**

With the merged tabular file containing all relevant annotations in a clean, structured format, we uploaded the file to RStudio for downstream filtering and prioritization. This final dataset enables us to apply systematic filtering criteria—such as rarity thresholds, damaging prediction consensus, and clinical significance—to identify a high-confidence set of variants most likely related to the condition of interest.

here we will do some R code to filter the file, As an end product for this step you are expected to include a nice table including at least 10 variants in your report that contains all relevant information for each of them, i.e. the chromomsome, position, reference and variant nucleotides, gene name and all relevant scores.

```{r}

snpFilteredVariants_1 <- snpFilteredVariants_1 %>%  
  filter(
    str_detect(ANN....EFFECT, "splice_region_variant|missense_variant"),
    #str_detect(ANN....IMPACT, "HIGH|MODERATE")
  )

#%>%
#select(
 #   -REF,

    #-FILTER, 
    #-ANN....FEATURE, 
    #-CLNVC

write.csv(snpFilteredVariants_Unique, "variants_Unique.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

# Discussion

The identified variants provide insight into the genetic basis of cardiomyopathy in the analyzed patient sample. While some variants occur in known cardiomyopathy-associated genes, further validation is required to assess their pathogenicity.


### Limitations

-   Analysis based on a single sample

-   Lack of functional validation

-   Potential sequencing and alignment biases

# Conclusion

This project demonstrates a reproducible workflow for variant discovery in cardiomyopathy using NGS data. The documented pipeline can be extended to additional samples and integrated with functional and clinical data for improved interpretation.
